content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides an overview of what constitutes a health-promoting school, emphasizing its role in fostering the physical, mental, and social well-being of students. This information is accessible on their official website. 2. A conceptual framework for addressing the social determinants of health has been outlined in a WHO discussion paper, which highlights actionable strategies to reduce health inequities. 3. Fernandes and Aurino conducted an economic analysis to identify an essential health package for school-aged children, as part of the third edition of Child and Adolescent Health and Development, published by the World Bank. 4. Sheehan et al. argue for global investment in adolescent capabilities as a foundation for sustainable development, presenting their case in a 2017 Lancet publication. 5. Strategies for improving health through schools, both at national and international levels, have been compiled and edited by Isolde Birdthistle, with resources available through WHO's digital repository. 6. WHO and UNESCO have collaborated to develop implementation guidance for making every school a health-promoting school, with the document currently in press. 7. The revised edition of UNESCO's International Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education provides an evidence-informed approach to comprehensive sexuality education. 8. UNICEF's 2012 manual on water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in schools serves as a companion to the Child-Friendly Schools initiative, offering practical guidance for improving hygiene practices. 9. WHO's guidelines on hand hygiene in healthcare settings provide evidence-based recommendations to reduce the risk of healthcare-associated infections. 10. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development includes new global indicators for monitoring access to safe drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene, as outlined in WHO's WASH-related publications. 11. Oral health promotion is recognized as a critical component of health-promoting schools, as detailed in WHO's school health information series. 12. Family life and reproductive health are identified as key elements of health-promoting schools, with guidance provided in WHO's school health documentation. 13. WHO and the World Bank issued a joint statement in 2003 on the importance of school deworming programs, emphasizing their role in improving child health and educational outcomes. 14. Malaria prevention and control are highlighted as essential responsibilities of health-promoting schools, with detailed recommendations available in WHO's school health series. 15. WHO has published a guide for introducing the HPV vaccine into national immunization programs, providing step-by-step instructions for implementation. 16. The WHO position paper on human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines, published in May 2017, outlines the organization's recommendations for their use in preventing cervical cancer. 17. The European Commission's 2018 report, Models of Child Health Appraised, evaluates various approaches to child health service delivery across Europe. 18. WHO's guidelines for the declaration of interests by experts ensure transparency and integrity in the development of health recommendations. 19. The PRISMA statement, developed by Moher et al., provides a standardized framework for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses, enhancing the quality and reproducibility of research. 20. Levinson et al. conducted a systematic review of reviews to assess the effectiveness of school health services delivered by healthcare providers. 21. Domitrovich et al. proposed integrated models of school-based prevention, combining logic and theory to address multiple aspects of student well-being. 22. Montgomery et al. systematically reviewed the effectiveness and acceptability of comprehensive, multi-component school health services, with findings published in the Journal of Adolescent Health. 23. The GRADEpro tool supports the assessment of evidence quality and the development of health recommendations, as outlined on its official website. 24. Rehfuess et al. integrated WHO norms and values with a complexity perspective in their 2019 publication in BMJ Global Health. 25. Sterne et al. introduced the ROBINS-I tool for assessing bias in non-randomized studies of interventions, published in BMJ in 2016. 26. The CASP checklist provides 12 questions to guide the evaluation of economic analyses, ensuring methodological rigor. 27. Thomas et al. discussed systematic synthesis methods in their book An Introduction to Systematic Reviews, edited by Gough, Oliver, and Thomas. 28. Balshem et al. outlined the GRADE guidelines for rating the quality of evidence in clinical epidemiology. 29. Guyatt et al. presented GRADE guidelines for upgrading the quality of evidence, emphasizing the importance of robust methodologies. 30. Lewin et al. described the application of GRADE-CERQual to qualitative evidence synthesis, providing a framework for assessing confidence in findings. 31. Atkins et al. discussed grading the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations in a 2004 BMJ article. 32. Guo et al. evaluated the impact of school-based health centers on children with asthma, highlighting improvements in health outcomes and cost savings. 33. Rodriguez et al. demonstrated the role of school nurses in asthma management, reducing absenteeism, and achieving cost savings in a 2013 study. 34. Van Cura explored the relationship between school-based health centers and reduced early dismissals, contributing to increased seat time for students. 35. Walker et al. investigated the impact of school-based health center utilization on academic outcomes, with findings published in the Journal of Adolescent Health. 36. Kocoglu and Emiroglu examined the effects of comprehensive school nursing services on students' academic performance in a 2017 study. 37. Guo et al. assessed the impact of school-based health centers on students with mental health problems, reporting significant benefits in Public Health Reports. 38. Siegel and Krieble evaluated high school health services, providing insights into their effectiveness in a 1987 study. 39. Guo et al. conducted a cost-benefit analysis of school-based health centers, highlighting their role in reducing healthcare disparities. 40. Roos et al. performed a cost analysis of a school health room, demonstrating partial financial benefits in a 1984 study. 41. Wang et al. conducted a cost-benefit study of school nursing services, published in JAMA Pediatrics in 2014. 42. Hutchinson et al. reported on the role of school-based health centers in improving adolescent health in post-Katrina New Orleans. 43. Svebak et al. evaluated the health effects of implementing school nursing in a Norwegian high school, using a controlled study design. 44. Wade et al. documented improvements in health-related quality of life among elementary and middle school students using school-based health centers. 45. Borge et al. assessed the status and future visions for school health services in Northern Tanzania, as reported by local healthcare workers. 46. Gibson et al. measured the impact of school health centers on access to and quality of primary care, with findings published in the Journal of Adolescent Health. 47. Strolin-Goltzman examined the relationship between school-based health centers and the learning environment, emphasizing their positive influence. 48. Zaghloul et al. analyzed the utilization patterns of a school health insurance program in Alexandria, Egypt, highlighting its impact on student health. 49. Frikha Jarraya et al. explored adolescents' expectations of school health services in Sfax, Tunisia, providing valuable insights into their needs. 50. Afifi investigated the association between adolescents' use of health services and mental health problems in Alexandria, Egypt. 51. Kumar et al. compared healthcare-seeking behaviors among adolescents in two service delivery models in India, identifying key differences. 52. Borges et al. studied service utilization among adolescents with suicidality in Mexico City, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions. 53. Otwombe et al. examined gender differences in health-seeking behaviors among adolescents in Soweto, South Africa. 54. Abdullah et al. evaluated school health services for primary school students in Holy Karbala, Iraq, identifying areas for improvement. 55. Ardahan and Erkin surveyed teachers' opinions on school nurses in private and public schools, highlighting their perceived roles and challenges. 56. Salehi et al. assessed the implementation of the school health nursing process in elementary schools in Kerman, Iran. 57. Yoo et al. evaluated the self-assessed competencies of school nurses in Korea, identifying areas for professional development. 58. Dibakwane and Peu documented the experiences of school health nurses in delivering services in the Tshwane district of South Africa. 59. De Oliveira et al. explored students' perceptions of the Health at School program in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, through a case study. 60. Silva et al. described the implementation of a health program in a Brazilian school, emphasizing its impact on student well-being. 61. Baggio et al. reported on the introduction of the school health program in Cascavel, Paraná, Brazil, from the perspective of nurses. 62. Brasil et al. discussed the complexity of integrating health and education in adolescent health promotion through the school health program. 63. Leite et al. examined teachers' perceptions of the school health program, identifying its strengths and challenges. 64. Peu et al. highlighted the challenges faced by healthcare providers in delivering school health services in the Tshwane sub-district of South Africa. 65. The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989, emphasizing the importance of child health and well-being. 66. WHO's Universal Health Coverage (UHC) compendium outlines health interventions to achieve universal health coverage. 67. WHO's guidelines for responding to child maltreatment provide technical recommendations for the health sector. 68. Global standards for quality health-care services for adolescents offer a framework for improving service delivery and outcomes. 69. The WHO Commission on Ending Childhood Obesity published its final report, outlining strategies to address this global health challenge. 70. WHO's recommendations on child health provide evidence-based guidelines for improving health outcomes in children. 71. WHO's interventions on water, sanitation, and hygiene aim to prevent diarrheal diseases, with resources available on their website. 72. WHO's operational guidance for maintaining essential health services during the COVID-19 pandemic offers practical recommendations for healthcare providers. 73. WHO's guidelines on diet and physical activity interventions provide evidence-based strategies for promoting healthy behaviors. 74. WHO's recommendations on adolescent health outline effective actions for improving health outcomes in this population. 75. The global strategy for women's, children's, and adolescents' health (2016–2030) emphasizes the importance of coordinated efforts to achieve health equity. 76. Promoting physical activity in schools is identified as a critical component of health-promoting schools, with guidance provided by WHO.
